lines.text: A write is acknowledged once a subset smaller than a quorum has it: the leader, and the leader alone.
The leader is then destroyed. Does the write genuinely survive?

tolerated.line: A write is acknowledged once a subset smaller than a quorum has it: the leader, and the leader alone.
The leader is then destroyed. Does the write genuinely survive?

lines.text: No, it genuinely gets lost.
The acknowledgement promised nothing more.
Run it for real: the write was genuinely lost, once the leader that alone held it was destroyed.
An acknowledgement smaller than a quorum promises nothing more, once the one node holding it is gone.

tolerated.line: Run it for real: the write was genuinely lost, once the leader that alone held it was destroyed.

lines.text: Now the leader durably records the write to its own disk before acknowledging, still with no replica involved.
The leader is destroyed the same way. Does durably recording it on the leader alone protect the write this time?

tolerated.line: Now the leader durably records the write to its own disk before acknowledging, still with no replica involved.
The leader is destroyed the same way. Does durably recording it on the leader alone protect the write this time?

lines.text: No, it genuinely gets lost too.
It never left the one node destroyed.

tolerated.line: It never left the one node destroyed.

lines.text: Run it for real: the write was genuinely lost again, even though it was durably recorded, because it never reached any node beyond the one that was destroyed.
Now the write is persisted by a real quorum instead: the leader, and enough replicas that any two quorums are guaranteed to overlap.
The identical leader destruction happens. Does the write survive this time?

tolerated.line: Now the write is persisted by a real quorum instead: the leader, and enough replicas that any two quorums are guaranteed to overlap.
The identical leader destruction happens. Does the write survive this time?

lines.text: Yes, genuinely.
A real quorum already held a second copy.
Run it for real: the write genuinely survived, on the identical leader destruction, because a real quorum already held a durable copy beyond just the leader.

tolerated.line: Run it for real: the write genuinely survived, on the identical leader destruction, because a real quorum already held a durable copy beyond just the leader.

lines.text: One real production messaging system's own documentation states the weakest of these policies directly.
Does it name a leader failing right after acknowledging on its own, before any follower replicates the record, as something that genuinely loses it?
Yes, it genuinely does.
That exact loss, named directly, in writing.

That system's own documentation states it in exactly those words: should the leader fail immediately after acknowledging the record but before the followers have replicated it, the record will be lost.
That same system's own documentation also names the real setting that turns a quorum requirement into an enforced guarantee.
It states that this setting causes the system to raise an error whenever the in-sync set falls below it.
So here's the shape of this whole topic: which single point in a replication pipeline counts as acknowledged genuinely decides whether a write survives the node that accepted it being destroyed.
A subset smaller than a quorum, even one that's durably recorded, can lose that write outright, since the data never genuinely left the one node that held it.
A real quorum cannot lose it the same way, because destroying any single node, even the leader, can never take every real copy with it.
